content: Central venous catheters (CVCs) in neonates are associated with serious complications, including thromboses, pericardial effusions, extravasation, and infections. Indwelling catheters are a significant risk factor for hospital-acquired infections. The use of antiseptic solutions during skin preparation for central catheter insertion is thought to reduce the risk of catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSI) and central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI). However, the optimal antiseptic solution for minimizing infection risk while avoiding adverse effects remains unclear. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the safety and efficacy of various antiseptic solutions in preventing CRBSI and related outcomes in neonates with CVCs. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-RCTs conducted in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). Trials comparing any antiseptic solution (alone or in combination) to another antiseptic solution, no antiseptic solution, or placebo were eligible. Cross-over trials and quasi-RCTs were excluded. The Cochrane Neonatal standard methods and the GRADE approach were used to assess the certainty of the evidence. Three trials were included in the review, involving 466 neonates from level III NICUs. Two trials compared 2% chlorhexidine in 70% isopropyl alcohol (CHG-IPA) to 10% povidone-iodine (PI), while one trial compared CHG-IPA to 2% chlorhexidine in aqueous solution (CHG-A). All included trials were at high risk of bias, and the certainty of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate. No trials compared antiseptic solutions to no antiseptic solution or placebo. CHG-IPA versus 10% PI: CHG-IPA may result in little to no difference in the incidence of CRBSI compared to PI (risk ratio [RR] 1.32, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.53 to 3.25; risk difference [RD] 0.01, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.06; 352 infants, 2 trials, low-certainty evidence). CHG-IPA may result in little to no difference in all-cause mortality compared to PI (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.68; RD −0.01, 95% CI −0.08 to 0.06; 304 infants, 1 trial, low-certainty evidence). The effect of CHG-IPA on CLABSI is very uncertain (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.07 to 15.08; RD 0.00, 95% CI −0.11 to 0.11; 48 infants, 1 trial, very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain regarding the risk of chemical burns with CHG-IPA compared to PI (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.24 to 4.48; RD 0.00, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.03; 352 infants, 2 trials, very low-certainty evidence). One trial indicated that CHG-IPA was associated with a lower risk of thyroid dysfunction compared to PI (RR 0.05, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.85; RD −0.06, 95% CI −0.10 to −0.02; number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome [NNTH] 17, 95% CI 10 to 50; 304 infants). Neither of the two trials assessed premature central line removal or the proportion of infants or catheters with exit-site infections. CHG-IPA versus CHG-A: CHG-IPA may result in little to no difference in the rate of proven CRBSI compared to CHG-A (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.87; RD −0.05, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.13; 106 infants, 1 trial, low-certainty evidence). CHG-IPA may result in little to no difference in the rate of CLABSI compared to CHG-A (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.34 to 3.84; RD 0.02, 95% CI −0.12 to 0.15; 106 infants, 1 trial, low-certainty evidence). CHG-IPA probably results in little to no difference in premature catheter removal compared to CHG-A (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.26 to 3.19; RD −0.01, 95% CI −0.15 to 0.13; 106 infants, 1 trial, moderate-certainty evidence). CHG-IPA probably results in little to no difference in the risk of chemical burns compared to CHG-A (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.47 to 2.03; RD −0.01, 95% CI −0.20 to 0.18; 114 infants, 1 trial, moderate-certainty evidence). No trial assessed all-cause mortality or the proportion of infants or catheters with exit-site infections. Conclusions: Compared to PI, CHG-IPA may result in little to no difference in CRBSI and mortality. The evidence is very uncertain regarding its effects on CLABSI and chemical burns. However, CHG-IPA was associated with a statistically significant reduction in thyroid dysfunction compared to PI. Compared to CHG-A, CHG-IPA may result in little to no difference in the rates of CRBSI, CLABSI, chemical burns, or premature catheter removal. Further research is needed, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, to determine the most effective and safe antiseptic solution for neonates undergoing central catheter insertion.
